variants.title: Circuit tester: an iron nail
variants.sample: Iron nail, 6 cm long and 2 mm across
variants.note: Resistance worked out as rho L / A for the piece between the probes: 9.71e-8 ohm m x 0.06 m / 3.142e-6 m2 = 0.0019 ohm, far less than the bulb's own resistance, so the bulb is as bright as with the probes touching.

source.title: Kaye & Laby, Tables of Physical and Chemical Constants: electrical resistivity of iron at 20 C, 9.71e-8 ohm m

variants.title: Circuit tester: an aluminium strip
variants.sample: Aluminium strip, 6 cm long and 2 mm across

source.title: Kaye & Laby, Tables of Physical and Chemical Constants: electrical resistivity of aluminium at 20 C, 2.65e-8 ohm m

variants.title: Circuit tester: a nichrome wire
variants.unknown: how much a resistance wire dims the bulb
variants.note: 1.09e-6 ohm m x 0.30 m / 7.79e-8 m2 = 4.20 ohm. This is as large as the bulb's own resistance, so the current is halved and the bulb is clearly dimmer: a conductor, but a poor one.

source.title: Published resistivity of Ni80Cr20 nichrome at 20 C, 1.09e-6 ohm m; SWG 30 diameter 0.3150 mm (BS 3737 standard wire gauge)

variants.title: Circuit tester: a piece of dry wood
variants.sample: Dry wood (its resistance is measured here, not looked up)
variants.note: Wood's resistivity runs over many decades with how dry it is, so no table value is used: this piece simply showed about 300 ohm on the tester. That is enough to keep the bulb completely dark while the meter still shows a few milliamperes.

source.title: Measured on this sample in the simulation; no published constant is claimed for wood
